records.title: Joint Model Partitioning and Bandwidth Allocation for UAV-Assisted Space–Air–Ground–Sea Integrated Network: A Hybrid A3C-PPO Approach

identity_evidence.quote: Received: 28 January 2026 Revised: 14 March 2026 Accepted: 14 March 2026 Published: 18 March 2026

primary_full_report.rationale: This 25-page primary research article formulates joint DNN model partitioning, terminal priority scheduling, and bandwidth allocation via a hybrid A3C-PPO framework evaluated in simulation (Sections 3–5, pp. 5–23).
primary_full_report.quote: Therefore, in this paper, we design a joint optimization framework based on Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) and proximal policy optimization (PPO).

multi_uav_evaluated.rationale: Section 5.1 (p. 15) configures three hovering UAVs with four intelligent terminals connected to each UAV, and Section 5.2 p. 21 separately introduces a single-UAV three-terminal Only-PPO component ablation that does not contradict Section 5.1. However, Section 5.2 main hybrid A3C-PPO plots (Figs. 6–7, pp. 19–20) omit simulated UAV counts, 12-terminal totals, and per-UAV results, describe A3C parallelization via worker threads or processes (p. 19), and describe the A3C-PPO-identical environment as four intelligent terminals connected to the UAV (p. 20), leaving actual multi-UAV execution in the main evaluation unconfirmed.
multi_uav_evaluated.quote: The experimental environment is configured identically to that of the A3C-PPO framework. Four intelligent terminals are connected to the UAV. Inference tasks are continuously generated by each terminal.

collaborative_inference.rationale: The evaluated DNN workload partitions ResNet18 layer-wise between an intelligent terminal and its nearest associated UAV MEC server (Section 3.1, p. 6; Table 3, p. 17; Eq. 1, p. 7), without modeled inter-UAV partitioning, task migration, or base-station/cloud inference execution despite Figure 1 (p. 6) drawing a three-tier schematic. Section 4.3 (p. 13) assigns one UAV to host a global A3C policy network and remaining UAVs as worker agents for RL coordination alongside Algorithm 1 (p. 15) training updates, but Section 5.2 does not verify runtime inference collaboration or orchestration across a multi-UAV-edge/cloud hierarchy.
collaborative_inference.quote: During deployment, one UAV serves as the central node hosting the global policy network for coordinated decision-making, while the remaining UAVs act as worker agents responsible for local state collection and policy sampling.

evaluative_evidence.rationale: Section 5.2 (pp. 16–23) provides simulation evaluations of ResNet18 cut-point latencies (Table 3, Figs. 3–4), PPO vs. random and brute-force partitioning (Fig. 5), A3C-PPO vs. AC-PPO and DDPG-PPO convergence (Fig. 6), Only-A3C/Only-PPO ablations (pp. 20–21, Figs. 7–8), learning rates (Fig. 9), and terminal priority scheduling (Fig. 10).
evaluative_evidence.quote: The effectiveness of the proposed A3C-PPO hybrid architecture is verified through comparative experiments. Two baseline strategies are constructed for evaluation. The bandwidth allocation strategy based on A3C is denoted as Only-A3C.

date_window.rationale: Publisher metadata on page 1 explicitly states Published: 18 March 2026, within 2021-01-01 through 2026-11-25.
date_window.quote: Received: 28 January 2026 Revised: 14 March 2026 Accepted: 14 March 2026 Published: 18 March 2026

english.rationale: The complete 25-page MDPI Entropy article is written in English.
english.quote: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV)-assisted mobile edge computing is pivotal for the Space–Air–Ground–Sea Integrated Network (SAGSIN) to support heterogeneous task offloading.

records.primary_reason: Unresolved gates: multi_uav_evaluated, collaborative_inference (Section 5.1 specifies three UAVs with four terminals each and p. 21 Only-PPO is a separate single-UAV ablation, but Section 5.2 omits multi-UAV/12-terminal counts and per-UAV results in main A3C-PPO plots and describes the A3C-PPO-identical environment on p. 20 as four terminals connected to the UAV; additionally, ResNet18 partitioning is modeled strictly per terminal-to-nearest-UAV pair and Section 4.3/Algorithm 1 A3C coordination is not verified as runtime multi-UAV inference orchestration in Section 5.2).

alignment.rationale: Sections 3.1, 4.3, and 5.1 (pp. 5–6, 13, 15) describe a three-UAV SAGSIN MEC architecture with A3C global/worker policy coordination and terminal-to-UAV ResNet18 layer partitioning, whereas Section 5.2 (pp. 16–23) does not verify multi-UAV runtime inference execution or cross-UAV orchestration beyond single-terminal/single-UAV latency plots, convergence curves, and component ablations.
alignment.quote: Three UAVs are deployed in the UAV-assisted edge network under SAGSIN scenarios. UAVs hover at heights of 40–100 m above ground to execute predefined tasks. The network coverage area is 500 m × 500 m.

unresolved: Missing main-evaluation multi-UAV reporting: Section 5.1 (p. 15) specifies three UAVs with four intelligent terminals per UAV, whereas Section 5.2 (pp. 16–23) omits simulated UAV counts, 12-terminal aggregates, and per-UAV breakdowns in Figs. 6–7, attributes A3C parallelization to worker threads or processes (p. 19), and describes the A3C-PPO-identical Only-A3C environment as four terminals connected to the UAV (p. 20); the separate single-UAV three-terminal Only-PPO experiment (p. 21, Fig. 8) is a baseline ablation and not a contradiction of Section 5.1.

Unresolved runtime inference collaboration scope: Equations (1)–(8) (pp. 7–9) and ResNet18 partitioning (Table 3, p. 17) model a terminal-to-nearest-UAV two-part split without inter-UAV partitioning or formulated base-station/cloud inference (contrasting with the schematic Partition 3 base-station box in Fig. 1, p. 6), and Section 5.2 does not establish whether A3C global/worker coordination (Section 4.3, p. 13; Algorithm 1, p. 15) performs multi-UAV runtime inference orchestration beyond RL training.

Reproducibility/provenance limitations: Section 5.2 (p. 19) omits the hardware platform and simulator details used to measure ResNet18 local/UAV execution times, and Data Availability (p. 24) states data are available on request due to restrictions.

Editorial/typographic observations (distinct from scientific evaluation): p. 5 retains meta-text phrasing about standard SCI paper organization, pp. 18 and 23 use chapter wording, Fig. 1 (p. 6) prints FeatureFinal, and Fig. 2 (p. 13) contains label typos (Partitlion, Channel Ganin, Date Size).
Title discrepancy: supplied input title_hint uses abbreviated UAV-SAGSN whereas the published PDF title reads UAV-Assisted Space–Air–Ground–Sea Integrated Network: A Hybrid A3C-PPO Approach (p. 1).

records.title: Adaptive Heuristics for Scheduling DNN Inferencing on Edge and Cloud for Personalized UAV Fleets

identity_evidence.quote: Adaptive Heuristics for Scheduling DNN Inferencing on Edge and Cloud for Personalized UAV Fleets

primary_full_report.rationale: Supplied PDF is a 50-page primary research preprint (arXiv:2412.20860v2, 24 April 2025, non-peer-reviewed) proposing DEMS, DEMS-A, and GEMS scheduling heuristics for multi-drone DNN inference. Under protocol 4.1(7), preprints are eligible only when providing unique recent evidence and labelled as non-peer-reviewed; supplied evidence contains no peer-review or Future Generation Computer Systems journal metadata, does not establish publication or version equivalence with the unverified input lookup DOI 10.1016/j.future.2025.107874, and does not verify the unique-recent-evidence exception.
primary_full_report.quote: We propose a deadline-driven heuristic, DEMS-A, to schedule diverse DNN tasks generated continuously to perform inferencing over video segments generated by multiple drones linked to an edge, with the option to execute on the cloud.

multi_uav_evaluated.rationale: Section 8.1–8.6 (pp. 23–32) evaluates 2–4 buddy drones per edge container (14–28 drone containers across 7 edge containers per host) and weak scaling up to 84 drone containers across 28 edge containers on 4 host machines.
multi_uav_evaluated.quote: We replicate the earlier setup of running 3D-P for 21 drones on one host machine (HM) to 21 drones each on 4 host machines simultaneously. This has a peak of 84 drones supporting 28 VIPs using 28 edge containers hosted on 4 machines.

collaborative_inference.rationale: Schedules six vision DNN models (HV, BP, DEV, DEO, CD, MD; Table 1, p. 23) continuously across buddy-drone video streams, Jetson-profiled edge containers, and AWS Lambda cloud FaaS via task dropping, edge-to-cloud migration, cloud-to-edge work stealing, and QoE-aware rescheduling (Sections 3–6, pp. 9–20).
collaborative_inference.quote: We use strategies like task dropping, work stealing and migration, and dynamic adaptation to cloud variability, to fully utilize the captive edge with intelligent offloading to the cloud

evaluative_evidence.rationale: Section 8 (pp. 22–37) evaluates VIoLET container emulation with Jetson Nano benchmarks and live AWS Lambda FaaS against seven baselines (Sec. 8.3), latency/bandwidth shaping with SUMO/NS3 mobility traces (Sec. 8.5), weak scaling (Sec. 8.6), sleep-emulated QoE GEMS runs (Sec. 8.7), and a single-drone Tello plus Jetson Orin Nano campus trial (Sec. 8.8).
evaluative_evidence.quote: We collect real video feeds on campus using the Tello drones and stream these from the drone containers to their base station containers. Our software platform, scheduler logic, and gRPC service hosting the DNN models run on each edge container.

date_window.rationale: Isolated arXiv stamp on page 1 explicitly states arXiv:2412.20860v2 [cs.DC] 24 Apr 2025, within 2021-01-01 through 2026-11-25.

english.rationale: All 50 pages of the arXiv preprint are written in English.
english.quote: Drone fleets with onboard cameras coupled with computer vision and DNN inferencing models can support diverse applications, from package deliveries to disaster monitoring.

records.primary_reason: Unresolved gate: primary_full_report (supplied PDF is non-peer-reviewed preprint arXiv:2412.20860v2 dated 24 Apr 2025 without journal publication metadata; under protocol 4.1(7), neither unique recent evidence nor publication/version equivalence with unverified input lookup DOI 10.1016/j.future.2025.107874 is established by supplied evidence).

alignment.rationale: Orchestrates deadline- and QoE-driven scheduling of multi-drone vision DNN inference tasks across edge accelerators and cloud FaaS using EDF prioritization, edge-to-cloud migration, work stealing, and WAN variability adaptation (Sections 3–8, pp. 9–37).
alignment.quote: We extend our DEMS solution to GEMS to solve this. We evaluate these strategies, using (i) an emulated setup of a fleet of over 80 drones supporting over 25 VIPs, with real DNN models executing on pre-recorded drone video streams, using Jetson Nano edges

unresolved: Preprint eligibility and version linkage under protocol 4.1(7): supplied 50-page PDF is arXiv:2412.20860v2 [cs.DC] dated 24 Apr 2025 (non-peer-reviewed preprint) and lacks Future Generation Computer Systems journal metadata or DOI 10.1016/j.future.2025.107874; neither publication status, version equivalence between arXiv v2 and the unverified input journal DOI, nor whether this preprint qualifies as unique recent evidence is established by supplied evidence.
Title discrepancy: supplied input title_hint ends in for UAVs whereas the supplied PDF title ends in for Personalized UAV Fleets (p. 1).

Study-family linkage: extends prior conference paper cited as [22] (IEEE/ACM CCGrid 2023 on DEMS, pp. 6, 9, 41) and application platform [2] (CHI 2023 Extended Abstracts on Ocularone, pp. 9, 39), and cites companion preprints [55] (arXiv:2504.03709) and [56] (arXiv:2504.01988) on p. 43.

Evaluation realism boundary: multi-drone evaluations up to 84 drones use VIoLET container emulation with Jetson Nano benchmarks, live AWS Lambda FaaS, and NS3/SUMO mobility traces (Secs. 8.1–8.6), Sec. 8.7 replaces DNN execution with sleep timers (p. 32), and Sec. 8.8 field validation uses a single DJI Tello drone with one Jetson Orin Nano edge (pp. 35–37) rather than a physical multi-UAV flight fleet.
